report:
**Conclusion: yes.** EMDR can alleviate PTSD symptoms and is an evidence-based, trauma-focused psychotherapy. It is not a guaranteed cure, and results vary by person, trauma history, co-occurring conditions, treatment completion, and clinician training.

**Evidence:** A Cochrane review of psychological treatments for chronic PTSD in adults found that trauma-focused therapies were effective; EMDR was among the treatments evaluated. This supports EMDR over waitlist/usual care, though psychotherapy studies can have limitations such as small samples, differing treatment formats, and difficulty blinding participants/therapists.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003388_psychological-therapies-chronic-post-traumatic-stress-disorder-ptsd-adults

A more recent individual-participant-data meta-analysis specifically compared EMDR with other psychological therapies, assessing PTSD-symptom reduction, response/remission, and dropout—an appropriate high-level design for judging comparative effectiveness.  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/psychological-medicine/article/emdr-v-other-psychological-therapies-for-ptsd-a-systematic-review-and-individual-participant-data-metaanalysis/903183C014DD518979569C26525588E1

**Guidelines:** NICE recommends EMDR as a trauma-focused treatment option for adults with PTSD, delivered in a structured manner by trained practitioners.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng116/chapter/Recommendations

The 2023 VA/DoD guideline likewise includes EMDR among recommended trauma-focused psychotherapies for PTSD, alongside prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy.  
https://www.healthquality.va.gov/guidelines/MH/ptsd/VA-DoD-CPG-PTSD-Provider-Summary.pdf

So, your “yes” is well supported: EMDR is a mainstream first-line or recommended option for PTSD, with evidence broadly comparable to other trauma-focused therapies—not clearly superior for everyone.
